---
title: "Setup"
description: "Install Miniforge, create the course environment, and get the course files onto your laptop before day 1."
---

Do this **before** the first session. It takes 15-30 minutes, most of it
waiting for downloads. If something fails, bring the error message to the
setup check at the start of day 1.

You need:

- a laptop with macOS, Linux, or Windows 10/11 (through WSL2)
- about 5 GB of free disk space (the environment is most of it)
- `git`, a terminal, and a text editor you like (VS Code, RStudio, vim, ...)

## 1. Install Miniforge

Miniforge is a small conda installer that uses the conda-forge channel by
default. If you already have Miniforge, Mambaforge or Miniconda, skip to step 2.

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

### macOS

Open Terminal and run:

```bash
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
```

Accept the license, keep the default location (`~/miniforge3`), and answer
`yes` when it asks to initialize conda. Close the terminal and open a new one.

On an Apple-silicon Mac (M1 and later), read the
[Apple-silicon note](#apple-silicon) before step 3.

### Linux

```bash
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
```

Accept the license, keep the default location (`~/miniforge3`), and answer
`yes` when it asks to initialize conda. Open a new terminal.

### Windows (WSL2)

Bioconda tools do not run on Windows directly, so you work inside Linux
through WSL2. In PowerShell **as administrator**:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
```

Restart when asked, open **Ubuntu** from the Start menu, and pick a Linux user
name and password. From now on, run every command of the course in that
Ubuntu window, then follow the Linux steps:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git curl
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
```

Keep the course files in your Linux home folder (`~/`), not under `/mnt/c/`:
Snakemake checks file times constantly, and the Windows drive is many times
slower from inside WSL. VS Code with the *WSL* extension edits files in the
Linux home directly.

:::

Check that conda works:

```bash
conda --version
```

## 2. Get the course files

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/jpflores-13/snakemake-course.git
cd snakemake-course
```

`--recurse-submodules` also fetches the lab pipelines (MicroCPipe, TTpipe,
ChromSimPipe) into `pipelines/`, which the field guide reads. If you cloned
without it:

```bash
git submodule update --init --depth 1
```

The course data in `data/` are small (a 5 Mb window of chr8) and come with the
repository.

## 3. Create the course environment

One environment holds Snakemake and every tool the lessons use:
[`envs/course.yml`](envs/course.yml).

```bash
conda env create -f envs/course.yml
conda activate snakemake-course
```

Run `conda activate snakemake-course` in every new terminal you use for the
course.

### Apple silicon {#apple-silicon}

We checked every package in `envs/course.yml` against the bioconda and
conda-forge package indexes (November 2026). All of them have native Apple
silicon (`osx-arm64`) builds **except `bioconductor-plotgardener`**, which
bioconda builds only for Intel Macs (`osx-64`) and Linux. So on an M1/M2/M3/M4
Mac, `conda env create -f envs/course.yml` stops with
`bioconductor-plotgardener does not exist`.

Build the whole environment for Intel instead. It runs through Rosetta 2,
which is a little slower but fine for the course data:

```bash
softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license   # once per Mac
CONDA_SUBDIR=osx-64 conda env create -f envs/course.yml
conda activate snakemake-course
conda config --env --set subdir osx-64   # later installs into this env stay Intel too
```

Only the `locus_plot` rule needs plotgardener. Everything else in the course
would also run in a native environment, so if you prefer native tools, you can
create the environment from a copy of `envs/course.yml` without the
plotgardener line and run the locus plot on Linux or the cluster.

## 4. Check the versions

```bash
snakemake --version          # 8.27.1
python --version             # Python 3.12.x
samtools --version | head -1
bowtie2 --version | head -1
macs3 --version
bedtools --version
bamCoverage --version
fastqc --version
dot -V                       # Graphviz, draws the DAG
Rscript -e 'suppressMessages(library(plotgardener)); packageVersion("plotgardener")'
```

The only version that has to match exactly is Snakemake's. Then do a dry run
of the finished course pipeline. It reads the samplesheet and checks that all
inputs exist, without running any tool:

```bash
cd course-pipeline
snakemake -n --cores 1 -s workflows/RegPipe.snakefile
```

The last line should be `This was a dry-run (flag -n). The order of jobs does
not reflect the order of execution.` If you get there, you are ready.

## Cluster users

Day 1 runs on your laptop. Module 5 moves the pipeline to a SLURM cluster; you
only need this part if you want to follow along there.

::: {.panel-tabset group="cluster"}

### Longleaf (SLURM)

The lab pipelines' `profiles/longleaf/` assume your own Miniforge in your home
directory, the same way as on a laptop. Log in, then:

```bash
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/jpflores-13/snakemake-course.git
cd snakemake-course
conda env create -f envs/course.yml
conda activate snakemake-course
conda install -c conda-forge -c bioconda "snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm>=1.0"
```

The SLURM executor plugin is what lets Snakemake submit each job with
`sbatch`. Module 5 sets up the profile in `course-pipeline/profiles/longleaf/`.

### Your own cluster

Any SLURM cluster works the same way: Miniforge in your home directory, the
course environment, and the executor plugin.

```bash
conda activate snakemake-course
conda install -c conda-forge -c bioconda "snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm>=1.0"
```

What changes between clusters is the account, partition names and limits.
Those live in a profile, not in the pipeline: module 5 starts from
`course-pipeline/profiles/slurm-template/` and shows you which lines to fill
in. Ask your cluster's documentation or admins for the partition names and
whether jobs need an account. For a scheduler other than SLURM, see the
[executor plugin catalog](https://snakemake.github.io/snakemake-plugin-catalog/).

:::

[Module 5: Running on a cluster](lessons/05-cluster.qmd) covers profiles,
resources, and the launcher script.

## If something goes wrong

`conda env create` is slow or seems stuck
: Solving an environment with R and Bioconductor takes a few minutes. If it
  runs for more than 15, make sure you are on a recent conda
  (`conda update -n base conda`) and that `~/.condarc` does not add the
  `defaults` channel.

`snakemake: command not found`
: The environment is not active. Run `conda activate snakemake-course`.

`snakemake --version` prints something other than 8.27.1
: Another Snakemake comes first on your `PATH` (for example from `pip install
  --user`). `which snakemake` should point into
  `.../envs/snakemake-course/bin/`.

The dry run says `MissingInputException`
: Something in `data/` is missing. Run `git status` and `git pull` in the
  course folder and try again.
